newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin in saddle, to score home, foreign firsts.
newsitem.headline: Jospin in saddle, to score home, foreign firsts.

text.p: Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, fresh from forging a tricolour "Red-Pink-Green" coalition, settles down to the business of government at home and abroad on Thursday.

The silver-haired premier will lead his broad-left government into its first encounter with conservative President Jacques Chirac, and then immediately heads off to Sweden to make his debut on the international stage.

For Chirac, humiliated by a stunning defeat for the former centre-right coalition in Sunday's snap parliamentary election, the first cabinet meeting will be a trying introduction to "cohabitation", or power-sharing.

"I felt as if I was surrounded by men of whom 60 percent hate me and 80 percent are fighting me. I was alone this morning, very alone," the late Socialist President Francois Mitterrand said of his first cabinet session with then-premier Chirac in 1986.
Surrounding Chirac on Thursday will be a young government featuring Socialists, Communists and Greens and giving a major role to women.
After the cabinet meeting, Jospin, 59, will make his first official trip abroad, going to the Swedish city of Malmo for a gathering of Socialist heads of government and parties.
He will address the conference on Friday and hold talks with Britain's new Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair, who swept to power in a landslide a month ago.
At two apparently harmonious meetings with Chirac, Jospin drew up on Wednesday the left-wing coalition brimming with new faces born of Sunday's upset win.

Of 14 senior ministers, five are women with Martine Aubry, 46, the daughter of former European Commission president Jacques Delors, taking the number two slot in charge of a superministry of employment and social security.
"That shows that jobs is the priority for this government," Manuel Valls, an aide to Jospin, told reporters.

In a gesture of goodwill to Chirac, Jospin appointed two non-confrontational Socialists to the key foreign affairs and defence portfolios, dealing with areas in which the president has a big say under "cohabitation" power-sharing.
Hubert Vedrine, 49, a former Mitterrand top aide and diplomatic adviser with long experience of managing "cohabitation", will be foreign minister.

The Communists returned to government for the first time since walking out on the Socialists in 1984. Former railwayman Jean-Claude Gayssot took the transport portfolio and his party comrade Marie-George Buffet, one of the new, female faces, becomes youth and sports minister.
Greens leader Dominique Voynet, an anti-nuclear campaigner and single mother whose ecologist party won its first seats, took the environment and regional development brief.
Jean-Pierre Chevenement, founder of the anti-Maastricht leftist Citizens' Movement, who resigned as defence minister in protest at the Gulf War, was named interior minister.
But Socialist officials made clear that he and the Communists would have to accept the government's pro-European line in support of a single European Union currency.

The Communist Party has not said what, if any, assurances it had obtained on its demands. These include a higher minimum wage and speedy implementation of promises to create 700,000 youth jobs and cut the working week to 35 hours from 39 to attack record 12.8 percent unemployment.

Elisabeth Guigou, 50, a cool technocrat with a strong background on European issues, was surprisingly named to the sensitive job of justice minister. Jospin aide Pierre Moscovici was given the European affairs portfolio under Vedrine.
New finance minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn drafted the Socialist economic policy which includes pledges to cut the working week to 35 hours from 39 with no loss of pay.

Chirac's own authority has come under fire on the right, with a chorus of Gaullists demanding the immediate removal of defeated ex-prime minister Alain Juppe as leader of his RPR party and the heads of several of the president's closest aides.
